units.translation: The letters di are contracted into ζ in the forms of the words ζαπρέπων [conspicuous] and κάρζα [heart] for διαπρέπων [conspicuous] and καρδία [heart], which see.

Etym. Gud. p. 227, 40. Etym. MS. Paris. in Larcherus in the Acts of the Parisian Academy of Inscriptions vol. 47 (or in Sturz's Appendix to Orion p. 213) and Gaisford p. 1161, and the grammarian codex Oxon. in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 2 p. 443. Ζαγρεὺς [Zagreus], the one who hunts greatly, as (ὦ [O] Oxon.) πότνια γῆ Ζαγρεῦ τε θεῶν πανυπέρτατε πάντων [O revered Earth and Zagreus, highest of all gods], the author of the Alcmaeonis said (πάντων – ἔφη [all – said] om. Oxon.). But some say that Zagreus is the son of Hades, as Aeschylus in Sisyphus (ἐν Σκύφῳ [in Scyphus] om. Oxon.) Ζαγρεῖ τε νῦν με (μοι [to me] Oxon.) καὶ πολυξένῳ χαίρειν [to Zagreus and to the hospitable one, greetings]. But in the Egyptians (sic Cramerus after Larcherus. αἰγυπτί [Egyptian] Oxon. αἰγύπτῳ [Egypt] Gud. and Paris.) thus he calls him (οὕτως αὐτὸν διὰ [thus him through] om. Oxon.) Pluto, the rustic, the most hospitable, because of the dead. Which Hermann corrected thus: Ζ. ὁ. μ. ἀ. [Zagreus, the one who hunts greatly] “πότνια Γἢ – πάντων [O revered Earth – all],” as the author of the Alcmaeonis, as Aeschylus in Sisyphus (fr. 229) “Ζαγρεῖ τε νῦν με καὶ πολυξένῳ πατρὶ χαίρειν [to Zagreus and to my hospitable father, greetings].” But in the Egyptians he thus calls him Pluto. Then another excerpt follows: in the Suppliants (147) he calls Zeus, “τὸν γάϊον, | τὸν πολυξενώτατον | Ζῆνα τῶν κεκμηκότων [the earth-born, the most hospitable Zeus of the dead].
